title: Parity subgraph-counting dichotomy
formal:
Is the following statement true? For every computable class \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple graphs whose matching-split number is unbounded, the parameterized problem \(\oplus\mathrm{Sub}(\mathcal H)\) is complete for parity-\(\mathrm W[1]\) under deterministic fixed-parameter Turing reductions:
\[\oplus\mathrm{Clique}\ \leq^{\mathrm{fpt}}_T\ \oplus\mathrm{Sub}(\mathcal H)\ \leq^{\mathrm{fpt}}_T\ \oplus\mathrm{Clique}.\]
The input to \(\oplus\mathrm{Sub}(\mathcal H)\) is a pattern \(H\in\mathcal H\) and an arbitrary host graph \(G\); its output is the parity of the number of subgraphs of \(G\) isomorphic to \(H\), and its parameter is \(|V(H)|\). No closure property beyond invariance under isomorphism is imposed on \(\mathcal H\). This is the parity clause of the source conjecture, using the reduction convention made explicit in the later classification paper.
why: A classification by a single structural parameter would identify exactly which graph-pattern families avoid the difficulty of parity counting, subject to the usual separation between fixed-parameter tractability and parity clique. This is a broad boundary theorem for counting complexity: taking counts modulo two can make families tractable even when exact counting remains hard. The unresolved scope is all computable pattern classes, beyond the substantial hereditary and tree cases.
status_note: The 2021 source’s definitions, Theorem 2 and Conjecture 14, together with the full 2024 Algorithmica paper’s Theorems 4–5, reduction definitions and conclusion, were read on 2026-09-14. sentences: The problem asks which graph-pattern families make counting copies modulo two parameterized-hard.
The proposed boundary is whether deleting a bounded number of pattern vertices always leaves only edges and isolated vertices.
Every computable class on the unbounded side is conjectured equivalent to parity clique under deterministic fixed-parameter Turing reductions.
Copies are ordinary unlabelled subgraphs, and the input pattern size is the parameter.
The classification is known for hereditary classes and classes of trees, while the general class-wide assertion remains the target.

definitions:
All graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and simple, given explicitly by their vertex counts and adjacency matrices. Empty graphs and isolated vertices are permitted. A graph class is computable if one deterministic algorithm halts on every finite graph and decides membership. It is invariant under isomorphism: relabelling vertices does not change membership. The class is fixed when defining its counting problem, rather than supplied as part of an instance.

For a graph \(H\), define
\[s(H)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq V(H),\ \Delta(H[V(H)\setminus S])\leq1\}.\]
Here \(H[U]\) is the induced graph on \(U\), and \(\Delta\) is maximum degree, with value zero for the empty graph. Thus deleting a splitting set leaves disjoint edges and isolated vertices. Unbounded matching-split number means
\[\forall B\in\mathbb N\ \exists H\in\mathcal H:\ s(H)>B.\]
The corresponding bounded condition is existence of one constant \(B\) working for all patterns in the class; it is not a bound that may grow with the input pattern.

Let \(\mathrm{Sub}(H,G)\) consist of pairs \((U,F)\) with \(U\subseteq V(G)\) and \(F\subseteq E(G[U])\) for which the graph \((U,F)\) is isomorphic to \(H\). Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving both adjacency and nonadjacency between those two graphs. The output is \(|\mathrm{Sub}(H,G)|\bmod2\), in \(\{0,1\}\). Each pair is counted once, regardless of the number of isomorphisms to it. Copies need not be induced in \(G\), and no labels or colors constrain embeddings. In particular, counting injective maps instead of copies would change this parity problem. Inputs are promised to have \(H\in\mathcal H\); algorithms and reduction oracle calls need only meet this promise, so no runtime charge for deciding membership in the fixed class is imposed.

The reference problem \(\oplus\mathrm{Clique}\) takes a graph \(G\) and a positive integer \(k\), outputs the parity of the number of \(k\)-element vertex subsets with all pairs adjacent, and has parameter \(k\). A deterministic FPT Turing reduction from a parameterized problem \((P,\kappa)\) to \((Q,\lambda)\) is one deterministic oracle Turing algorithm that computes the exact output of \(P(x)\) in time \(f(\kappa(x))(|x|+1)^c\). Here \(f\) is a total computable function and \(c\) is a constant. Every query \(y\) to \(Q\) satisfies its input promise and \(\lambda(y)\leq g(\kappa(x))\) for a total computable \(g\). The reduction may make adaptive queries and combine their returned bits; writing query strings and all other work are charged to the runtime. Oracle answers themselves have unit cost.

Completeness in this card means the displayed two reductions. For each fixed class \(\mathcal H\), the reduction algorithms, computable bounds and constant exponents may depend on \(\mathcal H\). No single procedure taking a membership-decider code and synthesizing these reductions is required. The explicit Turing convention follows Sections 2.3–2.3.1 of Goldberg–Roth. A single-instance parsimonious reduction, which would preserve the output without multiple oracle calls, is not an additional requirement. Fixed-parameter tractability means an exact deterministic algorithm of time \(f(k)(N+1)^c\) for total input length \(N\), a total computable \(f\), and a constant \(c\) independent of \(k\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universally quantified completeness statement with these counting and reduction conventions. A positive proof must cover every computable pattern class with unbounded matching-split number, including classes that are neither hereditary nor classes of trees. A negative proof must establish failure of the statement for a qualifying computable class; one tractable class would refute it only together with whatever class-separation fact is needed to rule out the required reduction. No unproved separation between FPT and parity-\(\mathrm W[1]\), or exponential-time hypothesis, is an assumption of the requested completeness theorem. Showing hardness of exact counting, counting embeddings, or induced-subgraph counting alone does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: The 2021 paper proves tractability for bounded matching-split number and asks for hardness throughout the complementary region. Its modular-counting conjecture has a separate clause for moduli with odd factors; that separate target is not included here.

Goldberg and Roth establish the completeness conclusion for every hereditary pattern class of unbounded matching-split number and for every recursively enumerable class of trees with that property. A hereditary class is closed under taking induced subgraphs. Their full journal paper includes the tree classification, which is absent from the shorter ICALP 2023 extended abstract.

These completeness results are unconditional reductions. The consequence that the hard problems are not FPT requires a complexity assumption; the paper uses the randomized Exponential Time Hypothesis, which rules out bounded-error randomized \(2^{o(n)}\)-time algorithms for \(n\)-variable 3-SAT. That conditional consequence is distinct from the requested completeness statement.

The full journal paper’s conclusion explicitly retains the general conjecture after proving the hereditary and tree cases. This card follows its deterministic Turing-reduction convention, avoiding an unstated demand that all hardness proofs preserve parity through just one output instance.
